Business.title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking
Business.text:
For some, networking comes naturally but for others, the thought of approaching someone they don't know and trying to make a professional connection can fill them with dread.

Whether you're looking for your first job, trying to get ahead at work or hoping to change career, building a network can help you find opportunities and make connections.

Networking doesn't have to mean working a room at a formal event - it can happen in person over a coffee at work, through a chance conversation or online, through email and social media.

Just under half (44%) of Gen Z say not having the right network is the biggest barrier to landing an entry-level role, according to research from LinkedIn, external.

Nicole Leverich, chief communications officer at LinkedIn, shares her top tips on how to network and we took the same question to city workers in New York to find out what has worked for them.

Everyone can start building their network online and "you'd be surprised how many connections you have once you connect with people you went to school with, former professors, people you met through summer jobs, family and friends," says Leverich.

Don't be discouraged if your network is small as "not having a network right now doesn't mean you'll never have a network", she says.

And not having obvious industry contacts shouldn't put you off.

Leverich grew up in a small town in Oregon and moved to San Francisco after college without knowing anyone who worked in communications.

After getting her first job, she says, "I raised my hand for a lot of the grunt work that other people didn't want to do and I built connections as I went along."

If you're thinking about reaching out to someone online, the key is to show you've done your homework, Leverich says.

In a message you should "reference something they've posted or establish some common ground".

Make sure your request is "clear and specific" and something they can do in less than five minutes. And, most importantly, don't forget to say thank you.

"You'd be surprised by how many people are willing to help, but I get so few thank yous," she says. "I'm not talking about anything excessive but just a 'thanks' makes you want to help next time."

Networking can feel transactional, so to avoid that, try to build relationships before you need something from them, Leverich advises.

If you know you want to work in a particular industry, "start finding people in that field a year or two before you're looking for a job".

When you reach out to them, think about what you can offer them in return.

"If you call me and say you want a job randomly, I'm much less likely to help than if you call and ask for five minutes of advice."

You also don't have to start by messaging someone directly, she says. Instead you could react to a post or drop a comment.

In-person networking can be more daunting, particularly early in your career, but remember that at a networking event, everyone is there to talk.

To begin a conversation, start with something simple like complimenting someone's outfit, introducing yourself and asking why they're there, Leverich advises.

"Put in the reps and start by going to an event for just 15 minutes or half an hour and then build from there."

When you want to move on, don't overthink it: "I just do the hard cut and say, 'It was great to meet you and I need to make sure I work around the room.'

"If you want a softer out, something like 'I need to get a glass of water, it was great meeting you' can work."

Of course, knowing what you're supposed to do is one thing but actually walking up to a stranger and starting a conversation, or even messaging someone out of the blue online, is another.

Taylor Crow who works in sales says she's "fairly good" at networking as it was something she prioritised at university.

"I sent over 200 cold DMs (direct messages) on LinkedIn and reached out to people in the companies I wanted to work at while I was studying."

She admits it was "so awkward" but it was something she had to do to land the job she wanted.

Her colleague Vicky Peterlin, 24, agrees. "It's not about being good at networking but more about not being afraid to reach out to people.

"I had thoughts about how I'm not qualified to have these conversations but then you realise there are no rules and sending out emails and messages are free and easy.

"The worst that can happen is that they say no and that's ok."

Katherine Leopold, a careers and employability tutor at Greenwich Business School, echoes this. She says the biggest hurdle is making the first move but if you don't take the step you are "ruling yourself out".

The number of applications that organisations are dealing with is "absolutely enormous" so try to meet employers in person and show them your total authentic story, she advises.

"Ensure you say to them, 'I have this skill, I have this piece of knowledge, so I'm confident that your team is stronger with me in it.'"

He gets a lot of young people reaching out to him for career advice and opportunities, and says many of them could be much clearer in what they are looking for.

"There's nothing wrong with saying what your goal is or what you want to get out of this interaction."

He adds that it's important to be yourself and "more doors will open if you are authentic".

Business.title: Warren Buffett steps down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway after over 50 years
Business.text:
Warren Buffett is stepping down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway, the company that he took from a faltering textile manufacturer into a $1tn conglomerate over the course of 60 years.

Buffett’s son, Howard, 71, will take over as chair. Buffett, 96, cited his age as the main reason behind the transition, noting that he has a one-year-old great-grandchild who is “moving a bit faster than I am these days”.

“Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted,” Buffett, 96, said in a letter to shareholders. “Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead.”

Buffett said he will remain as chair emeritus and a director on the board. He left his post as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway in May 2025, shocking the audience of thousands at the company’s annual shareholder meeting in Omaha, Nebraska. Greg Abel, vice–chair of the company, replaced him as CEO.

Known as the “Oracle of Omaha”, Buffett built a reputation as a sharp-eyed investor, building up Berkshire Hathaway into a $1tn conglomerate. The company owns dozens of companies in construction, manufacturing, consumer goods and insurance, along with being a major investor in some of the biggest companies on the stock market, including Nvidia, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta.

Bloomberg places Buffett’s net worth at $145bn, making him the 10th richest person in the world.

Howard Buffett, known as “Howie”, is Buffett’s second child out of three and was long planned to be his father’s successor as chair of the company, having served on the board since 1993.

“He is getting it because he’s my son,” Buffett told the Wall Street Journal in January 2025. “I’m very, very, very lucky in the fact that I trust all three of my children.”

In a statement, Abel said that Buffett’s impact on the company “is without parallel in the history of American business”.

“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian,” he said.

Business.title: Workers in New York seek to create first AutoZone union as company resists
Business.text:
Workers at an AutoZone in White Plains, New York, are seeking to become the first store at the US’s largest auto parts retailer to win a union election, set to begin 25 September, despite a heavy-handed union opposition campaign from the company.

LaborLab, a non-profit workers’-rights watchdog, estimates AutoZone has spent around $200,000 to oppose the unionization effort at the White Plains store, where 11 workers are eligible to vote to join the United Auto Workers Local 259. The estimate is based on external attorney costs and internal costs of executive salaries based on reports from workers at the store.

AutoZone did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

The company has more than 6,800 retail stores in the US and reported a net income of $2.5bn in fiscal year 2025.

Nathan DuCongé has worked at an AutoZone store in White Plains, New York, for about two years, where he started as a sales associate making minimum wage.

“I just remember that being very low, but I needed it very badly, and so I accepted the job,” said DuCongé. “For a job that just essentially pays minimum wage, it just makes no sense, that you’re doing all of this work, which essentially is service sales, and you’re also expected to upsell certain products too.”

He explained that the idea to unionize came from the low pay and working conditions, but took off after he attended an Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee training session and met an organizer with United Auto Workers.

David Valencia, who also works at the AutoZone store in White Plains, said he began working there in May 2026, and became interested in the union after being scheduled to work the Fourth of July holiday and did not receive any sort of holiday pay or bonus for doing so.

“When I got my paycheck and saw that they didn’t pay anything extra when part-time employees leave their families for holidays and sacrifice the time that they have with their families to come to work, you don’t get anything extra, any recognition, and that just blew my mind,” Valencia said. According to Indeed, AutoZone only provides paid holidays for eligible full-time employees.

“Our goal is to get compensation, job security, just more things that closely reflect the value that we know that we bring to the company. We’re not getting close to what we’re worth,” Valencia added. “There is no bargaining when you’re alone. They’re only going to bargain when you’re together. So we don’t have a choice. Either we’re going to live in poverty and not be able to pay our bills, or we’re going to do this.”

DuCongé and Valencia both explained that AutoZone management caught wind of the union organizing drive after they had collected enough union authorization cards to file for a union election with the National Labor Relations Board.

They said the following day, the store became filled with regional and corporate managers and human resources executives.

“They had sent in a whole fleet of managers, they were flying in people from around the country, and it was very bizarre, because even customers were kind of noticing how many managers were in the store,” said DuCongé.

He noted the response from AutoZone was initially asking how they could help, but switched to deterring unionizing after the group issued a letter to management announcing their intent to unionize.

“They were pulling people into the back. They had these long meetings where they would read: ‘Hey, we don’t think that the union is good. Here’s all the reasons why,’” said DuCongé.

He explained that AutoZone threatened to delay the union election by challenging DuCongé’s eligibility to participate. He says the issue caused the union election petition to be withdrawn initially in late July, then refiled in August.

“We essentially had no choice. If we wanted to get to an election, I had to sacrifice my eligibility as a worker,” he said.

DuCongé provided recordings where, he said, he is told by a manager “we will accept your invitation to fire you”, although DuCongé said he had never suggested that, and was told his social media posts were being monitored.

He also shared a screenshot of AutoZone CEO Phil Daniele’s Facebook account appearing as an account that had watched one of his social media stories about the union campaign.

Several letters from AutoZone management to workers plead for them to vote against the union, citing union dues and claiming “you could actually end up with less” because “nobody knows what tradeoffs will be made in bargaining” and “your wages could go up or down”.

The letters did not cite the existence of any proposed union contract where workers would end up with less pay, nor explain why AutoZone or the union would propose regressive pay in a contract.

“I believe local 259 will destroy the mutual respect, teamwork and culture you and I have built at store 2976,” one management letter states.

LaborLab, with the help of workers in the store, identified at least 11 corporate executives at AutoZone who have appeared at the White Plains, New York, store whom they say were there to deter workers from organizing, and several regional and district managers.

The Teamsters previously attempted to unionize an AutoZone distribution center in the early 1990s. They lost the election, though the National Labor Relations Board subsequently ordered a rerun election due to AutoZone’s conduct during the election, which included prohibiting union discussions at work, threatening workers with loss of their jobs and withholding scheduled pay increases.

“Seeing the amount of money, the managers, everybody that they’re sending in, it really kind of shows that you can make change at the store,” concluded Valencia. “You can make change within the company because the fact that you’re unionizing it and you’ve got this kind of a response is actually a good thing. It means that you really are out there changing things, and I believe that if we can do it, and hopefully we do win, then everybody else can too.”

Business.title: Trump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime falls
Business.text:
Spanish hotel chains. A Canadian mining firm. European shipping giants. Visa and Mastercard. Scores of foreign companies have been driven out of Cuba this summer over fear of being hit with potent, new secondary sanctions. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, told Axios last month there are “no escape valves” from his unprecedented pressure campaign against the island.

But not everybody is losing out. A growing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets, charging top dollar to help clients navigate the ever-expanding web of sanctions, and positioning themselves for lucrative business opportunities in the case of regime collapse.

Since an executive order signed by Donald Trump on 1 May drove Canada’s Sherritt International from its nickel and cobalt mining joint venture with the Cuban state, two rival US bids to buy out its stake have been presented to US authorities.

Ray Washburne, the vice-chair of Trump’s 2016 Victory Committee who organized last week’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, is clashing with Albert Huddleston, another Texas oil tycoon with close ties to the White House. Both are hoping to swoop in, despite nine-figure claims on Sherritt’s Cuba holdings by Citigroup and Office Depot – Fortune 500 corporations. Washburne did not respond to the Guardian and the consortium group including Huddleston declined to comment.

A similar approach is being pursued by Australia’s Antilles Gold Ltd, which after being blacklisted over its Cuba operations in June received the green light from the Trump administration to negotiate the transfer of its stake in a Cuban copper-gold mine to the New York-based, multibillion-dollar investment fund, Global Emerging Markets.

“If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail,” said a person with several decades of experience in Cuba policy who requested anonymity.

Sources tell the Guardian that several Trump Organization executives who had previously traveled to the island to explore real estate deals and who even registered the Trump trademark there in 2008 have in recent months returned to Cuba under the aegis of Dominari Holdings for meetings. The executives are said to have met with Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, the grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, dubbed “the Crab”, to explore opportunities amid the departure of Spanish hotel giants Meliá and Iberostar, which had been operating on the island since the 1990s.

Neither Antilles nor Dominari returned calls for comment.

But American investors aren’t the only ones sensing opportunity in Rubio’s effort to coerce the sanctions-battered country of his parents’ birth into becoming economically dependent on the US.

Cubans have been living under an effective fuel blockade since January 2026: the Trump administration cut oil shipments to the island from the island’s main ally after abducting Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan president; it then nixed oil deliveries from Mexico by threatening tariffs on any country sending petroleum to the island.

Treasury department-authorised oil exports from Florida and Texas to the island’s private sector, however – all but non-existent last year – have shot up to over $160m so far this year.

Meanwhile, Florida shipping lines such as Crowley, a donor to Cuban-American Republican lawmakers from Florida, Mario Díaz-Balart and María Elvira-Salazar, seem to be beneficiaries of fresh sanctions that have hit foreign shippers and forced Cuba-bound commerce to reroute through Florida, according to informed sources who spoke with the Guardian. Crowley declined to comment.

And as UN human rights experts warn that Washington’s latest measures “knowingly deprive a population of the means to survive”, Franklin Graham, the Trump-allied CEO of evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse recently secured a $40m federal contract to distribute humanitarian aid in Cuba – despite lacking the capacity to effectively implement such a contract on the island, according to sources familiar with the matter. A spokesperson for Samaritan’s Purse said: “Details about aid for Cuba are still being developed and are not yet finalized.”

Ironically, some of those who have called most vociferously for harsher sanctions are also cashing in.

In July, Madrid-based Vima World SL, a leading player in the island’s food industry which partners with GAESA, the Cuban military conglomerate that controls large swathes of the island’s economy and has become the main target of the US squeeze, hired top Washington lobbying firm Continental Strategy – led by Cuban-American allies of Rubio who oversaw the maximum pressure Cuba policy as officials in the first Trump administration – for matters related to trade, foreign relations and the food industry.

Continental’s executives include Carlos Trujillo, Trump’s former ambassador to the Organization of American States John Barsa, Trump’s former acting USAID administrator and Alberto Martinez, Rubio’s former chief of staff. The firm, which terminated its contract with Vima this month after netting nearly $40,000 according to corporate disclosures, has been known for providing lobbying and government relations services to clients staunchly opposed to the one-party state, including MasTec, the telecom company owned by Rubio’s friend Jorge Mas Santos; American Sugar Refineries, owned by Trump-ballroom donor and Rubio patron Pepe Fanjul; and General Cigar Co, which is fighting Cuba’s state-owned tobacco enterprise in US court for the rights to the Cohiba cigar trademark.

“It’s been interesting to watch how quickly some hardline ideologues become pragmatists once there’s money on the table,” one person familiar with the contract told the Guardian, noting that Continental has taken on other Spanish firms with Cuban business interests “trying to get on the right side of sanctions, like banks and hotel chains”.

Other organizations that for years have won seven-figure grants from US federal agencies are capitalizing on the Trump administration’s push to force sweeping political and economic change on the island.

Lobbying disclosure forms filed in July by a newly formed group made up of former employees at the US taxpayer-funded Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyist Otto Reich and the husband of top Rubio state department aide Viviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”.

Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, are involved in efforts to mobilize billions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC).

To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularly meets with state department officials and wants to become Cuba’s next leader, have paid DC lobbying firm The Cormac Group a combined $100,000 since December.

For another US taxpayer-funded non-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time.

Just before the July release of a heavily criticized state department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000 contract from the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main site launched an online interview series repeating Trump administration claims of Cuba’s purported threat to US national security.

Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment.

“The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”

Business.title: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada
Business.text:
Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”.

The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”.

Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength. In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

In response to Trump’s comments, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions.

“It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship ⁠with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad ‌told Public Sénat TV channel.

A European Commission spokesperson said: “As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of the relationship with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. After meeting EU leaders in Strasbourg on Wednesday, he described the EU and Canada as “natural partners, united by shared values” and said that both sides were focused on “a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples”.

An associate membership agreement would have to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states, who generally support closer ties with Canada, but were taken by surprise by the term.

Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU.

In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the ​US, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition.

The force is ​a rapid response ‌military partnership comprising 10 North Atlantic Nato member states including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.

On Wednesday, Carney and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, held a bilateral meeting at the ground of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves.

The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial ​intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance ​of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence.

The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However, it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market.

Von der Leyen said on Wednesday that it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.

She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

Sports.title: Portugal: Cristiano Ronaldo named in new coach Jorge Jesus' first squad
Sports.text:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football.

Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July.

But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October.

Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit.

The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years.

The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit.

When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head."

This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football.

Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028.

The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024.

Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea).

Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel: England boss on 'embracing the chaos' ahead of Nations League fixtures
Sports.text:
England manager Thomas Tuchel left the United States in July pining for greater control.

At his first squad announcement since the World Cup on Friday, the German spoke of "embracing the chaos".

Is it possible to have controlled chaos? It seems Tuchel is ready to find out.

England's third-placed finish in the US was the nation's best performance at the World Cup since 1966.

But the memories of the team's semi-final loss to Argentina linger.

In the aftermath of the heartbreaking defeat, Tuchel pointed to his team's inability to find control having taken the lead via Anthony Gordon's opener as a key factor behind his side's late collapse.

Fast-forward two months, however, and the messaging is rather different ahead of the four upcoming Nations League games.

"Football is about adapting to situations and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach, if you look at the 6-4 against France [in the World Cup bronze-medal match]," said Tuchel.

"But people talk about it like it's one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match, so maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best."

Mixed signals? Or maybe it is just a sign that Tuchel wants his side to become more unpredictable in their search for success.

Because that is what the best teams do - mix it up when required.

Despite Tuchel's remarks, his latest squad for the fixtures against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia rather contradicts any thoughts of a havoc-rich approach.

The return of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer, two of English football's most technically gifted players, screams control.

So do the call-ups of Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall, who are both extremely adept in possession of the ball.

Of course, there is certainly a balance to be struck. That would be Tuchel's ideal scenario.

Rio Ngumoha's first senior call-up will certainly add an air of unpredictability to Tuchel's options.

The Liverpool winger, 18, has had an exciting start to the season, catching the eye with his invention and trickery down both flanks for Andoni Iraola's side.

That Tuchel revealed Fulham attacker Josh King is also close to earning his first senior call-up provides further indication the England manager wants to reinvigorate his forward line ahead of the forthcoming Nations League campaign and beyond.

Yet, we shouldn't expect Tuchel to completely let go of the handbrake just yet.

In response to a question as to whether his team can replicate the fast-paced approach of a Premier League team but harnessed with a greater control, Tuchel responded: "That would be the wish, that we become for 10 minutes a little bit more like Spain, here and there.

"The more I reflect on it, it's maybe more buying into our strengths and play more minutes like we played the second half against Croatia, and more minutes like we played the first half against France, and buying into these strengths, because I think we get a lot of value out of it, we get a lot of connection to the fans, this is what the Premier League reflects.

"We are maybe not the most economical team to play football but this is maybe also a characteristic of the Premier League. The Premier League is not a very economical league, you have to play.

"You need to max out every single match otherwise you cannot compete for the title so this is something more beautiful. But this is where we are, where I am in my mindset and I think where the players are, so it's still a bit ambiguous."

But while Tuchel may not have total clarity with regards to whether control or chaos is the way forward, he showed no hint of confusion over who he believes his best players are.

Tuchel refuted assertions his decision to recall Palmer and Alexander-Arnold was an admission he'd got his World Cup squad wrong.

Indeed, Tuchel has hinted he would have picked a vastly similar squad for the upcoming games to the one he selected for the US had all his options been available.

"Before we did the nomination in the last month, I thought we had more of a continuation of the World Cup squad but then a lot of members of our World Cup squad - Reece [James], Dan [Burn], Dean [Henderson, [John] Stones, [Jordan] Henderson, Djed Spence - can't be with us due to injuries, so it is not like a full continuation.

"These players were crucial for us in building the brotherhood, in building the spirit and taking care of the mentality that took us the long way in the tournament. We will not negotiate on that, we will not give in on that.

"So other players will step up, this is basically how I see this camp.

"My mindset at the moment is not to change too much within the formations."

England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September then travel to the Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October.

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel: Man Utd youngster travels to Barcelona amid speculation over future
Sports.text:
Manchester United youngster JJ Gabriel has travelled to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature.

The 15-year-old has told United he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect.

BBC Sport reported on Thursday that Real Madrid have a firm interest in the forward, and Bayern Munich, Paris St-Germain and Barcelona are also known to be keen.

It is understood Gabriel left the UK on Thursday and went to France, but is now in Barcelona.

If United hold on to the Londoner's registration, it would stop him moving to another English club until the end of the season.

But if he obtains a European Union passport through either his father - a former Republic of Ireland international - or mother, who has Greek-Cypriot heritage, he could join a club in the EU when he turns 16 on 6 October.

Gabriel has not trained at United since scoring a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut on 10 September. Tournament rules prevent him from playing for a side other than United in this season's competition.

Sources close to Gabriel were furious the club did not register him for their Champions League opener with Sabah FK, which Michael Carrick's side won 4-0.

The United manager was again asked about Gabriel on Friday at his news conference to preview Sunday's Premier League match against Fulham.

"He's a young boy, JJ, and I think it's important we don't play anything out here," he said.

"With the exposure and scrutiny and everything, you got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything.

"The situation will work itself out, whatever way it's going to work itself out. Making sure he's OK is the important thing."

Gabriel scored in his first two Premier League 2 outings for United this season but will not be involved against Brentford at Leigh Sports Village on Friday.

Sports.title: Manchester United: Michael Carrick refuses to consider job fears
Sports.text:
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to start thinking how long he has left in the job after "two or three" bad results.

His side visit Fulham on Sunday after an awful week.

After United lost at home to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men after 23 minutes, Brighton became the first side to come from two goals down to win at Old Trafford in 50 years in their Carabao Cup tie.

United supporters responded to the midweek setback with boos and by chanting against their team.

Carrick said in the aftermath he was "not bothered" by the pressure - a sentiment he reinforced as he spoke to the media before the Fulham trip.

"I know the club, I know the role, I know what's expected here in terms of playing to a certain standard and achieving certain things on the pitch," he added.

"I get all that.

"In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, that's totally not in my thinking. It's ridiculous to think that way in the position I'm in, that's just not on the radar.

"It's two or three games. It's two or three games too many because I really hate losing, but that doesn't mean the world caves in. In some minds it does, it can't for us."

There has been no sense from senior figures inside United that Carrick's position is under threat. They are more focused on the perceived under performance of so many players given the 12 games out of 17 that were won under the 45-year-old over the second half of last season.

By contrast, they have two victories from six games so far, against newly promoted Ipswich - when they had to come from behind - and Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.

"It's not a catastrophe or a disaster," said Carrick. "It's not the end of the world."

Yet it is the measure of the noise around a club of United's size that is often feels that way.

Carrick accepted issues at Old Trafford are frequently amplified, so they look to be bigger than they actually are.

Despite this, he loves his job - and the club he served with such distinction as a player, and began his coaching career.

"There's great feelings, and there's obviously disappointments, and sometimes the smaller disappointments lead to being a little bit bigger," he added. "It's just part of coping and being at this great football club.

"I wouldn't want to be anywhere else, genuinely.

"It's the best place for me to be, in part because of the times when it's maybe not going to plan. Sometimes they are best times to work your way through, to find out a few things and come out an awful lot stronger."

Externally, the inquests have tended to focus around recruitment - or lack of it, specifically at left-back - United's finances and debt levels, Carrick's relative inexperience and, other than assistant boss Steve Holland, that of his coaches.

"It's not a blame game," said Carrick, who revealed Luke Shaw and new signing Carlos Baleba "have a chance" of being fit for the Craven Cottage meeting.

"We all search for things to look at and point at, or whatever reason it may be and find a blame. Blame me. No problem. I will take the responsibility.

"But it's not about blaming people. It's about us, it's about us finding solutions and being better. That's as a whole football club."

Sports.title: Uefa and Concacaf demand Fifa pays $10m to all 211 member countries
Sports.text:
Uefa and Concacaf have written to Gianni Infantino calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.

It is the latest chapter in the war of words between the governing bodies, in response to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's aborted private equity proposal.

Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to an investment company.

The idea was scrapped after four days following widespread opposition from national associations.

In its statement immediately after FFE was cancelled on 1 August, Uefa said that there should be no need for Infantino to sell off part of the game.

It outlined that "with reserves standing at over $5bn (£3.7bn), he has also failed to use associations' money for the benefit of the game".

Uefa has now called on Fifa to release part of those reserves to each country, at a cost of $2.11bn (£1.57bn).

This would be in addition to the regular funding in the 2027-30 cycle.

The news comes a day after Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt sent a letter to Infantino and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom demanding that all documents relating to the controversial plan were released.

Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

Infantino was told he should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October.

Sports.title: England v Canada: Sophie de Goede still loses sleep over World Cup final loss
Sports.text:
It is nearly a year since Canada lost the Women's Rugby World Cup final to England - but time has not been a healer for everyone.

"Four to five nights a week I can't fall asleep because I'm still thinking about the final," says Canada captain Sophie de Goede, who is preparing to take on the world champions this Saturday at Sandy Park in Exeter.

So, is this match revenge for the side ranked third in the world?

Canada head coach Kevin Rouet is keen to play this down: "Revenge is a good brand but they [England] won the final of the World Cup - that was the most important game to win, the next important games will be in the World Cup 2029."

After Canada, England play New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, before two more tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa. In recent history, England's women have never faced such tough successive opposition.

Red Roses head coach John Mitchell says the games are an "audition" for the 2029 World Cup.

"You look at the geography that we're going to cover, we're not always going to be in our training base. We're going to be going to different facilities. It's a challenge," he said.

"It's going to be really cool to see how they handle pressure as well. I think the Red Roses are very good around pressure because I think it reveals how much they care".

There continues to be misconceptions around the status of the Canadian women: they are professional athletes but contracts, as with most other nations, do not yet compare to England's women.

The Canadian programme involves a clever strategy of using England's domestic PWR league to develop its players.

There are 25 Canadians in PWR and the current Canada coaching staff includes Kevin Rouet and Alex Austerberry, who both coach Saracens Women, and Nathan Smith from Loughborough Lightning.

"It's not like we're coming in to spy," joked De Goede. "We just don't have the quality league [in Canada]."

Canada are not the only country to do this - PWR is littered with top internationals from across the globe.

Mitchell has told BBC Sport that he and Charlie Hayter, head of women's performance at England Rugby, have lobbied to increase PWR game time for English Qualified Players (EQP) from next season.

Mitchell has frequently pushed his theory that players who can reach 1,000 PWR playing minutes a season "gives them a higher probability" of playing for the Red Roses.

"I haven't enjoyed seeing young English players between 21 and 23 not getting enough minutes," he said.

"I think that number [1,000] is very meaningful."

The RFU confirmed to BBC Sport the current requirements around 13 EQP players on average across matchday squads will remain. However, the lure of signing foreign talent will be dampened by the removal of club injury credit, which helps cover the cost of replacing an injured player.

From the 2027-28 season, only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible.

Besides this, if any EQP player is captured by another union, they will only be able to hold their EQP status until the end of that season.

Sports.title: Liverpool: How Andoni Iraola is moving Reds on from Arne Slot era
Sports.text:
Only 12 months ago Liverpool had won each of their first five Premier League games and were seemingly on their way to defending their crown under Arne Slot.

That run started with victory over a Bournemouth side led by Andoni Iraola on the opening night of the season.

Surely no one thought then that, come the end of the campaign, Iraola would be replacing Slot at Anfield.

Such is the volatility of football, it is too early to pass judgement on Iraola - even if his Liverpool side are already six points worse off than they were at this stage last season.

Under the 44-year-old, Liverpool are still unbeaten and this weekend Iraola returns to the place he called home for three years.

It will certainly be an odd feeling when he enters the smaller away changing room at Bournemouth - the Cherries have had to renovate it to comply with Europa League regulations, so at least it will be a slightly more pleasant experience than it would have been previously.

Iraola has swapped the seaside on the south coast for the beach town of Formby, where former Liverpool managers Jurgen Klopp and Brendan Rodgers also resided. By all accounts, he is settling in well. He has been spotted in the city centre on a few occasions and, as a keen cyclist, has enjoyed the coastal routes.

But Iraola is most at home on the training ground. He is very much a 'six days a week' coach, according to those at Liverpool, and such is his passion for coaching that he is often the first on the training pitch, marking the cones out for sessions.

"It's really intense. There's a lot of hard work and no sort of light days. Everyone's putting in 100%," said forward Lewis Koumas.

Those at Liverpool are firmly of the belief that everyone associated with the club was glad to get last season out of the way and that even if Slot had remained as head coach, things were always going to feel better.

At Liverpool's AXA Training Centre in Kirkby, Iraola rarely uses his own office and is often found in the coaches room where his assistants in Tommy Elphick, Shaun Cooper and Pablo de la Torre are based, and he has a relatively low-key presence in and around the building, compared to previous managers.

De la Torre, who moved with Iraola from Rayo Vallecano to Bournemouth in 2023, is seen as a key pillar in ensuring that the players are all up to the physical standard that Iraola wants.

In terms of actual changes inside the club they are not as big as people may think from the outside, given the structured nature of the head coach role.

Iraola's appointment was based on his fine work at Bournemouth but he is very much learning on the job when it comes to dealing with Liverpool's congested schedule.

There is a willingness to listen to other departments like the medical and fitness teams at Kirkby as the Reds seek to manage a squad that will play at least 49 games this season - a number that could climb into the 60s depending on Liverpool's cup runs.

When it comes to the training schedule, Iraola tends to adapt it in line with the kick-off time for the following fixture, with late afternoon and early evening sessions increasingly common. Under Slot, Liverpool tended to train at a similar time each day.

There have also been conversations with the academy and Rob Page, who coaches Liverpool Under-21s.

"We have an understanding of how the first team play and key principles, like how we press, how he [Iraola] wants his number 10 to press, how he wants his number eight to press, how he wants his centre-backs to press - we mirror that absolutely," said Page.

Earlier this week, Dominik Szoboszlai explained how Liverpool play with a number six, a number eight and a number 10 - and, despite calls for a defensive midfielder from fans during the transfer window, Iraola's system can work if everyone improves collectively.

Iraola's preference is to name the team on the morning of the game and he saves the post-match debrief with his players for the day after the match.

There is a sense of pragmatism with his media interactions, too, after a situation where his comments to LFC TV following a pre-season friendly against Monaco were widely reported.

Iraola conceded Liverpool had run out of steam after 30 minutes and did not have the energy levels at the time to play with the intensity that he wants. It wasn't meant to be a dig at his players - rather an admittance that they were working on building that intensity up.

But there is a realisation that at a club like Liverpool, every word you say can end up shared across social media and taken in a different way than you meant. That said, Iraola comes across as calm in his news conferences and open to discussion.

It is very much a case of Iraola adapting to the club as much as the other way round.

One of the main reasons they went for Iraola was his ability to develop young talent and the average age of Liverpool's players in the Premier League this season is 25.3 - only five teams have a lower average.

Youngsters like Rio Ngumoha, 18, Trey Nyoni, 19, and Koumas, 20, all started against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup and all three will play bigger roles this season than last.

Intensity is a buzzword under Iraola and that is a non-negotiable but he is already aware that, with such a brutal schedule, Liverpool will need to find ways to adapt and occasionally win games with a set-piece or an individual moment of brilliance.

Going into this weekend, they have made the most sprints in the Premier League but looked flat against Fulham last weekend in a goalless draw, less than 72 hours after beating Atletico Madrid in the Champions League.

Sunday's game against Bournemouth will be a fourth in 12 days and, after the international break, Liverpool have a spell of four games in 10 days. Between 11 October and 7 November, they will play nine times.

Iraola would no doubt have had a smile seeing Bournemouth win on their Europa League bow against Real Sociedad on Thursday, in the Basque region where he grew up.

Perhaps he will have a moment on the flight down from Liverpool on Saturday to think about how far he has come.

Liverpool haven't exactly had a dream start under Iraola but they are yet to lose. Becoming a team that is hard to beat is undoubtedly a step in the right direction after 12 league losses last term, but as vice-captain Alisson said last week, draws aren't good enough for Liverpool.

And Iraola, who is unbeaten in the Premier League since January across his two clubs, knows that a win on familiar territory on Sunday would be the perfect way to head into the international break.

Sports.title: Finlay Tarling: Disgraceful nothing has changed - Matthew Brennan
Sports.text:
Britain's Matthew Brennan says it is "disgraceful that nothing has changed" in cycling to make the sport safer following the death of Fin Tarling last month.

Britain's Tarling, 19, died on 14 August during the Volta a Portugal following a high-speed collision with a van which had strayed on to the closed road.

His funeral took place in Aberystwyth on Thursday.

Brennan, 21, who races for Dutch team Visma-Lease a Bike, told BBC Sport: "It was very sad what happened with Fin. We were watching his funeral yesterday and I said to my friend: 'It's so sad we've lost someone so special and also nothing has changed.'

"I really think that is disgraceful. Instead of someone somewhere in these organisations saying: 'OK, this should never ever happen again', it feels the world has moved on, nothing has changed and there's events where cars have been on the course still."

Six riders have died during road races in the past three years, and American rider Ezra Caudell is currently in hospital, external with "multi-system trauma" following a crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

Brennan, who won five stages at the recent three-week Vuelta a Espana Grand Tour, believes there should be an independent body to force through safety requirements at races.

"It's unbelievable, because you've lost a friend and when nothing changes it is really shocking.

"I think these big organisations and [sport's world governing body] the UCI should have a look at what they need to do to increase the safety.

"In my personal opinion, there should be an independent organisation that holds the organisations, the UCI and everything accountable to some very strict rules that makes sure the safety of the riders is held as a priority."

The UCI has been contacted by BBC Sport for comment.

Earlier this month the UCI proposed the introduction of GPS trackers at all races to pinpoint riders' locations at all times.

The sport's biggest races, such as the three-week Tour de France, typically have a good safety record. This is thanks in part to extensive safety measures which include total road closures on stages for much of the day.

Smaller events such as the Volta a Portugal and Tour of Britain use 'rolling roadblocks', where police and officials travel in front of and behind the peloton.

Races such as the third-tier Volta a Portugal sell their rights to be broadcast at a lower fee than the bigger races and use more cost-effective measures to manage road closures.

However, Brennan, who also won the prestigious one-day classic race Kuurne-Brussels-Kuurne this year, believes the demands of the sport are changing as it grows, and was vocal at the recent Vuelta over racing in 44-degree heat.

"We have big outside factors such as TV ... I would say that's a massive one. The instances of racing in Spain, and instead of moving it forward to racing at 09:00 we're racing at 15:00 in the midday heat.

"I think a real independent organisation that can really say to the teams whether something is safe, or whether something needs to be changed would benefit the sport and hopefully would stop these sad tragic events that happened at World Championships [referring to Muriel Furrer in 2024] and what happened with Fin and all the other sad events that happen in the sport."

Sports.title: How the women's 800m became athletics' headline act
Sports.text:
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.

This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.

The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.

The progress, however, was temporary.

German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.

The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.

Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.

In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.

So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.

It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.

In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.

She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.

"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."

But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.

Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.

"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."

After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.

The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.

"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.

"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."

Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.

"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.

Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.

The next target was to go under two minutes.

"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).

It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.

She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."

In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.

Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.

"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.

"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."

From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.

But the 1983 record stands to this day.

It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.

Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.

In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.

Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.

At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.

Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.

"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.

"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."

"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.

"It's stronger than it's ever been."

Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.

The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.

Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.

She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."

Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.

"I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport.

"If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal: Barcelona star says he's experienced racism a thousand times
Sports.text:
Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal says he has experienced racism "a thousand times", because people are unaware their comments or behaviour are offensive.

The Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia, a government agency, said earlier this year that the 19-year-old and Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr were the most frequent targets of online racist abuse in Spain in the final quarter of 2025.

Lamine Yamal was among the Barca players targeted by racist abuse during El Clasico against Real Madrid at the Bernabeu in October 2024.

And in an interview with broadcaster Movistar, the winger, who helped Spain to win the World Cup in July, said he had encountered racism on a regular basis during his rise to prominence.

"A thousand times. People are indirectly racist toward you, but maybe don't realise it," he said.

"There are a lot of comments or looks that are racist and they don't even notice.

He added: "If someone calls me Black, it's not going to bother me at all, ultimately I'm Black, I'm not any other colour.

"Another thing is whether it's good or bad, whether they're saying it to offend me.

"But if I'm playing a match and they paid for a ticket to see me, I'm not going to get angry just because they disrespected me."

Sports.title: Josh Allen shines again as Bills celebrate new home with slugfest victory over Lions
Sports.text:
Josh Allen quickly put his stamp on the Buffalo Bills’ new stadium, which has been dubbed “The House that Allen built.”

Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores, and the Bills beat the Detroit Lions 41-31 on Thursday night in the first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium.

It was Allen’s fourth five-TD outing, and followed a four-touchdown outing (two passing, two rushing) in Buffalo’s season-opening win at Houston.

“[We won in a] short week against a really good team who kept us fighting until the last second there,” Allen said after the game.

Allen followed the pregame fireworks celebration with more of his own by overseeing touchdown drives on each of Buffalo’s first four possessions.

He scored the first regular-season TD in the stadium on a one-yard run 5:51 into the opening quarter. He followed that with a 43-yard scoring pass to a wide-open Josh Palmer. Tight ends Dalton Kincaid, with a 16-yard catch, and Dawson Knox, with a one-yarder, also scored for Buffalo in the first half.

Allen finished the night 20 of 31 for 248 yards, and added 72 yards rushing. James Cook had 134 yards rushing and put the game away with a one-yard TD run late in the fourth quarter.

“I got a little emotional during the national anthem, feeling super blessed and lucky to do what I do. This is a great spot, we’re going to be here for a long time, hopefully the fans enjoyed it,” said Allen.

Allen’s two rushing TDs upped his career total to 83, moving him into a tie for 18th on the NFL list with Jim Taylor. He also picked up his 90th regular-season victory, becoming one of just four quarterbacks to reach that milestone through their first nine seasons.

The Lions were undone by their injury-depleted defense, and a banged-up offensive line that had difficulty opening holes for Jahmyr Gibbs and protecting Jared Goff.

After rallying from a 21-0 deficit to cut Buffalo’s lead to 34-24, the Lions offense stalled midway through the fourth quarter. Backed up at their own 10, the Lions went three-and-out and were forced to punt after Goff had two passes tipped by Deone Walker, and Gibbs was stopped for no gain.

Goff finished 26 of 38 for 327 yards and four touchdowns. Amon-Ra St Brown had nine catches for 142 yards and two scores. Gibbs also scored on an 11-yard catch but was limited to 52 yards rushing. Sam LaPorta scored on a one-yard catch.

The Lions’ defense got off to a dreadful start, allowing the Bills to score 27 points and gain 299 yards in the first half alone. The struggles carried over from a season-opening 31-30 overtime win over New Orleans, in which the Saints rallied from a 21-0 first-half deficit and lost only after their two-point conversion failed in overtime.

The Lions’ troubles began on Buffalo’s second drive when two defenders converged on DJ Moore, allowing Allen to find Palmer wide open deep for a 43-yard touchdown. On Buffalo’s next drive, a holding penalty against Rock Ya-Sin, negated Skyler Gill-Howard’s interception of a tipped pass.

The Lions’ offense had its own sputters, with Goff sacked twice and also having a snap go over his head on Detroit’s first two series.

The $2.1bn Highmark Stadium that officially opened last month was built across the street from the Bills’ former home. The new stadium has a capacity of just over 60,000, about 12,000 less than the old facility. What’s different is the layout, with the new facility’s seating structure built steeper, placing viewers more on top of the action. The new building also features a canopy, which helps project crowd noise directly on to field.

Bills fans began arriving two and three days earlier, with a private lot nearly filled with RVs by Tuesday.

Sports.title: My son’s death during a college football workout was preventable. Lessons must be learned
Sports.text:
Late last month, Arizona State hockey player Matthew Mayich collapsed during a team workout. He is now fighting for his life after suffering from exertional heatstroke and, according to the Mayich family attorney, is unlikely to make a meaningful recovery. This young man was drafted by the St Louis Blues but will never get the opportunity to play in the NHL. While he is not the first young athlete severely harmed by heat-related illness in American sports, he should be the last.

I have learned more about this preventable injury than I ever wanted to know. On 29 May 2018, my son Jordan McNair collapsed during a strenuous football practice at the University of Maryland. By the time he arrived at the hospital, he was dangerously overheated and never recovered.

For two weeks, as Jordan fought for his life through intensive care and an emergency liver transplant, one question kept coming: “What did we miss?”

I think about the days before he signed with Maryland, when coaches sat at our kitchen table talking with our family about Jordan. I remember asking two questions:

“Can Jordan get some playing time?”

And, “What support do you have around mental health and substance abuse?”

Those are the kind of questions many parents ask when they have never experienced a life-changing tragedy in collegiate sports. Jordan was going to play football at a Big Ten university. What could possibly go wrong?

“If something happens to my son, what safety systems do you have in place?”

“What is your emergency action plan?”

“When was the last time you practiced it?”

“Who has the authority to stop a workout when an athlete is in medical distress?”

“What happens if my child suffers exertional heatstroke?”

“Where is the equipment needed to save his life?”

Those questions came in hindsight, as I walked toward the ICU every day while Jordan fought for his life. I kept asking myself:

“What did I miss that night at the kitchen table?”

Before Jordan collapsed, I thought heatstroke and heat exhaustion were one and the same. I thought if someone became overheated, you moved them into the shade, gave them water, let them cool down, and everything would be fine. I didn’t know a heat-related injury could kill my son. My education came through a baptism by fire.

Suddenly, as the Mayich family may be learning now, I had to understand medical terms I had never heard before: rhabdomyolysis. Core body temperature. Multiorgan failure. Exertional heatstroke.

Since Jordan’s death, I’ve worked alongside medical professionals to cool athletes experiencing exertional heat illness at sporting events across the nation. I’ve seen first-hand how quickly proper recognition and response can change an outcome.

One of the simplest explanations of exertional heatstroke has stayed with me. When your core body temperature rises above 104F (40C), it is like putting your body inside a microwave. Your organs begin to cook.

There is a critical window of roughly 20 to 30 minutes to rapidly cool the athlete and avert catastrophe. Cold-water immersion can bring the body’s temperature down before the damage becomes irreversible.

Time is everything.

But what happened to Jordan wasn’t only about what went wrong on the football field on 29 May 2018. What happened to Mayich in Arizona isn’t only about what happened on 20 August 2026. The tragedy began long before.

Every organization has layers of protection, and every layer can have weaknesses, the holes in the Swiss Cheese Model. One hole may not cause disaster because another layer can stop it. But when enough holes align, nothing remains between the athlete and tragedy.

There was an emergency action plan in Jordan’s case. But having an emergency action plan on paper and being prepared to execute it are two very different things. Imagine having a fire evacuation plan nobody ever practices. Then one day the building catches fire. Who knows where to go, what to do, who calls 911 and who gets people out? The middle of the fire is the worst possible time to figure out the plan. Athletic emergencies are no different.

Every time an athlete steps on to a field, court, track or practice facility, an emergency is possible. The systems designed to protect that athlete must be in place before it happens, and the people responsible for those systems must know exactly what to do.

I used to say Murphy’s law was in full effect the day Jordan collapsed. While I wasn’t in Arizona for the team practice where Matthew Mayich collapsed, reports from that day reveal unsettling parallels to my son’s case.

During a strenuous early-season workout, the athlete’s level of distress wasn’t properly recognized. The escalation from heat exhaustion to exertional heatstroke wasn’t appropriately addressed. The emergency action plan was not properly practiced or implemented. The lifesaving cooling response wasn’t initiated within that critical window. Necessary equipment wasn’t within immediate reach. Changes in the normal practice setting complicated the emergency response, and precious time was lost before treatment began.

One hole.

Then another.

Then another.

Until they aligned.

By the time Jordan arrived at the emergency room, more than an hour and a half after he collapsed, his core body temperature was approximately 106F. My son never came home.

Three days after Jordan died, on 16 June 2018, I began what would become my life’s work as a student-athlete safety advocate. There is a club of parents none of us ever asked to join. We are mothers and fathers who sent our children off to play the sports they loved and eventually had to bury them. We don’t need another member.

We certainly don’t need another parent standing outside an ICU asking the same question I asked myself over and over:

“What did I miss?”

My prayers remain with Matthew Mayich and his family. I pray they receive the outcome every parent outside an ICU desperately hopes for.

For years, I kept returning to the questions I asked at our kitchen table.

Now, I know the question I should have asked. “Can my child play and will my child be safe?”

Parents shouldn’t have to experience what my family has before they learn to ask that question. Medical professionals responsible for the health and safety of athletes shouldn’t wait until an athlete collapses to understand and practice their role in an emergency action plan.

Schools and athletic programs shouldn’t discover holes in their safety systems while a child’s life hangs in the balance. Coaches need to understand their role in that system without being expected to diagnose or treat a medical emergency. Athletes should never wonder whether speaking up about how they feel will be interpreted as weakness.

The on-field cardiac arrest of Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin demonstrates that having a disciplined emergency action plan goes beyond heat-related injury. Hamlin’s full recovery after immediate CPR and emergent cardiac defibrillation is an excellent example of how lifesaving intervention should be available for athletes at risk. He not only made it to the hospital; he walked out on his own and eventually returned to the playing field.

The NCAA, with over $1bn in revenue, owes its players that same level of emergency preparedness.

This is an opportunity for youth sports organizations at every level to have mandatory emergency action plans in place for the life-threatening emergencies their athletes face. This includes heat-related injury as well as other serious sports-related emergencies such as cardiac events, traumatic head injuries and complications of sickle cell disease.

Students, parents, coaches and administrators must hold athletic organizations accountable to have these resources in place because the next missed opportunity may be fatal.

Martin McNair is the father of Jordan McNair and founder of The Jordan McNair Foundation.

Gaming_Tech.title: Flight chaos caused by millisecond software defect, says air traffic control body
Gaming_Tech.text:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect"affectingthe system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."
